drills.q: How many patches does a 224x224 image split into 16x16 patches produce (before adding the CLS token)?
True or false: vision tokens fed into an LLM are discrete ids looked up in the same vocabulary table as text tokens.
drills.a: False -- vision tokens are continuous vectors produced by a vision encoder plus a projection layer, with no vocabulary entry and no decode() step.

drills.q: What was the batch size used in the original CLIP paper's pretraining, and why does batch size matter for contrastive pretraining?
drills.a: 32,768. A larger batch provides more and harder in-batch negatives per gradient step, since every non-matching pair in the batch is a free negative for the contrastive loss.

drills.q: A candidate says 'GPT-4o just converts the image to some tokens, it's basically free compared to text.' Correct this.
drills.a: A single 1024x1024 image in GPT-4o high-detail mode costs roughly 765 tokens (85 base + 170 per 512x512 tile) -- comparable to 500-800 words of text. It is not free; three or four such images can consume as much context budget as several pages of text, and vision tokens incur the same O(n^2) attention cost as text tokens.

drills.q: Explain why LLaVA-1.5 always produces exactly 576 vision tokens per image regardless of image content, and name one production consequence.
drills.a: LLaVA-1.5 always resizes input to 336x336 and uses a fixed 14x14 patch grid (24x24=576 patches), with a simple 2-layer MLP projecting each patch embedding independently -- no dynamic sizing. Consequence: a visually simple icon costs the same 576 tokens as a visually dense photo, and fine detail below one patch's spatial resolution is lost regardless of the source image's actual resolution.

drills.q: Why does a Vision Transformer need learned positional embeddings when a CNN's architecture doesn't require an equivalent mechanism?
drills.a: Self-attention is permutation-invariant by construction -- it has no inherent notion of which patch came from where. A CNN's convolution is inherently local and translation-equivariant, baking spatial structure into the architecture itself. ViT must explicitly add positional embeddings to each patch to recover spatial order information.

drills.q: Is Whisper a fused multimodal architecture in the same sense as LLaVA or GPT-4o's vision handling? Justify.
drills.a: No -- Whisper's audio encoder output doesn't share an embedding space with a downstream LLM by default. It's a standalone encoder-decoder producing discrete text tokens directly, typically integrated as a cascaded ASR-then-text pipeline, unlike a VLM which projects continuous vision embeddings directly into the LLM's own sequence for joint attention.

drills.q: A production RAG pipeline adding full-page document images alongside existing OCR'd text saw cost and latency roughly triple. Diagnose the cause and propose two fixes.
drills.a: Each full page image adds several hundred to 1000+ vision tokens on top of existing OCR text tokens, and vision tokens incur the same O(n^2) attention cost as text, so prefill latency scales worse than linearly. Fixes: (1) drop the raw image for pages where OCR text alone suffices, reserving image input for pages with important non-text visual content (tables, diagrams); (2) use low-detail/downscaled modes, or crop to only the specific regions OCR struggled with, instead of sending full-resolution full pages by default.

drills.q: Design the vision-token budget policy for an agentic browsing tool that screenshots every step of a multi-step task. What breaks without a policy, and what should the policy be?
drills.a: Without a policy, appending every step's full-resolution screenshot to growing conversation history burns roughly linear context purely on images (a 20-step task could hit 15,000-20,000 tokens on screenshots alone), risking hitting the context ceiling or unexpected cost. Policy: keep only the most recent 1-2 screenshots in context, drop older ones once acted on unless explicitly needed for comparison, use low-detail mode where fine text-reading isn't required, and summarize stale screenshot content into text once no longer the active focus.

drills.q: What is a CLIP typographic attack and why does it succeed? Does the vulnerability carry forward into VLMs built on top of CLIP?
drills.a: Pasting text onto an image (e.g. writing 'iPod' on a photo of an apple) shifts the CLIP embedding toward that word's semantic neighborhood strongly enough to flip zero-shot classification, because contrastive training never explicitly taught the model to distinguish depicted content from depicted text -- both correlate with caption text in training data. Yes, it carries forward into any VLM whose vision encoder is a frozen or lightly fine-tuned CLIP, unless the downstream LLM's own training independently learned to discount text-in-image, which isn't guaranteed -- a real prompt-injection-via-image attack vector.

drills.q: Explain the mechanical role of the projection layer in a VLM like LLaVA, and contrast its form with Qwen-VL's approach.
drills.a: The projection layer bridges the vision encoder's output dimension to the LLM's embedding dimension so the resulting vectors can be concatenated into the LLM's input sequence. LLaVA uses a simple 2-layer MLP with GELU, applied per-patch independently, always producing as many output tokens as input patches. Qwen-VL uses a merger module with 2D-RoPE-aware attention that can compress/merge adjacent patches, producing a variable token count rather than a fixed one-to-one mapping.
